hokkaido.label: Hokkaido
hokkaido.description: Located at Japan's northernmost tip, Hokkaido is vast and surrounded by sea, covering about 22% of Japan's total land area. It offers pristine natural scenery and fresh air — cool summers and a snow paradise in winter. The relaxed pace of life and relatively affordable costs make it ideal for students who want to escape big-city noise and focus on study while experiencing authentic Japanese life.
hokkaido.climate: Four distinct seasons: cool summers (20–26°C) and harsh, snowy winters (-10–0°C). A great region to experience snow country culture and skiing.
hokkaido.suitableFor: Students who love nature, want a quiet study environment, are interested in skiing or outdoor activities, or are working with a tighter budget.
hokkaido.lifeAccess: Sapporo has a subway and tram network with solid daily amenities. Suburban areas rely on buses, and winter travel can be disrupted by heavy snowfall — choosing a campus near the city center is recommended.

tohoku.label: Tohoku
tohoku.description: Tohoku covers the northern part of Honshu across six prefectures. Centered on Sendai, the 'City of Trees,' the region is rich in natural scenery, warm community spirit, and some of Japan's most authentic rural culture. Costs are among the lowest in Japan, making it ideal for students who want to immerse deeply in local life and experience traditional festivals like the Aomori Nebuta and Sendai Tanabata.
tohoku.climate: Distinct four seasons: mild summers (22–28°C) and cold, snowy winters (-2–5°C), with heavy snowfall on the Japan Sea side.
tohoku.suitableFor: Students who want an authentic, unhurried Japanese experience, have a limited budget, love traditional culture and festivals, or prefer warm, community-oriented surroundings.
tohoku.lifeAccess: Sendai is Tohoku's transport hub with Shinkansen access to Tokyo (about 1.5 hours) and a city subway. Other prefectures rely mainly on JR trains and buses.

kanto.label: Kanto
kanto.description: Centered on Tokyo, the Kanto region is Japan's political, economic, and cultural core — and the most popular destination for study abroad. It offers the widest selection of language schools, vocational schools, and universities in Japan, with unmatched transport links and daily conveniences. Anime, fashion, food, and subculture are all here, along with the most part-time work and internship opportunities in the country.
kanto.climate: Four distinct seasons: hot, humid summers (28–35°C) and dry, cool winters (2–10°C) with little snowfall.
kanto.suitableFor: Students who want big-city life, the widest choice of schools and job opportunities, an interest in anime, fashion, or subculture, or who want maximum part-time work options.
kanto.lifeAccess: Japan's most extensive rail network — JR, subway, and private lines woven together for effortless commuting. Daily life is impeccable, though rent and living costs are the highest in the country.

chubu.label: Chubu
chubu.description: Chubu spans nine prefectures including Aichi, Shizuoka, Niigata, and Ishikawa, centered on Nagoya — Japan's fourth-largest city and a key industrial hub (home of Toyota). Living costs are significantly lower than Tokyo or Osaka, with abundant industry internships and jobs nearby. It also sits close to Mt. Fuji, Tateyama Kurobe, and Kanazawa's Kenroku-en, blending urban convenience with natural and cultural beauty.
chubu.climate: Four distinct seasons: hot summers (28–34°C). The Japan Sea side gets heavy snow in winter; the Pacific side is dry and cool (3–8°C).
chubu.suitableFor: Students interested in manufacturing or engineering internships, those who want urban life on a smaller budget, or those who enjoy a balance of city amenities and natural surroundings.
chubu.lifeAccess: Nagoya is the region's transport hub with Shinkansen access to both Tokyo and Osaka. The city subway is well-developed, rents are reasonable, and overall value for money is high.

kansai.label: Kansai
kansai.description: Kansai is centered on Osaka, Kyoto, and Kobe — the cradle of Japanese history and culture. Kyoto preserves the elegance of a thousand-year-old capital, Osaka is famous for its bold commercial energy and food culture ('Japan's Kitchen'), and Kobe exudes the charm of an international port city. Living costs are slightly lower than Tokyo, with a wide range of language and vocational schools — perfect for experiencing traditional Japan without sacrificing urban convenience.
kansai.climate: Four distinct seasons: hot, humid summers (29–35°C) and cool winters with little snow (3–9°C). Kyoto's basin geography makes its summers hotter and winters colder.
kansai.suitableFor: Students who love Japanese traditional culture and history, enjoy great food, want city life at lower rent than Tokyo, or have an outgoing personality and love meeting people.
kansai.lifeAccess: A dense web of JR, Hankyu, Keihan, and subway lines makes travel between Osaka, Kyoto, and Kobe a quick 30–60 minutes. Daily amenities are excellent, and Kansai locals are famously warm and sociable.

chugoku.label: Chugoku
chugoku.description: Chugoku covers the western end of Honshu across five prefectures. Hiroshima is an internationally recognized symbol of peace, home to the UNESCO-listed Atomic Bomb Dome and Itsukushima Shrine. Okayama is renowned for its high number of sunny days and pleasant climate. With mild weather, lower living costs, and a relaxed pace, it suits students who want to focus in a quiet environment while engaging with rich history and culture.
chugoku.climate: The Seto Inland Sea side has mild, low-rain weather (among Japan's sunniest areas). Four distinct seasons: summers 28–33°C, winters 4–9°C.
chugoku.suitableFor: Students who prefer a mild climate, quiet study environment, interest in historical sites and World Heritage sites, or a tighter budget.
chugoku.lifeAccess: Hiroshima has trams and buses, with Shinkansen connections to Osaka and Fukuoka. Daily amenities are sufficient, and rents and living costs are affordable.

shikoku.label: Shikoku
shikoku.description: Shikoku consists of four prefectures — Tokushima, Kagawa, Ehime, and Kochi — and is Japan's smallest main island region. It offers beautiful natural scenery and unique cultural heritage including the 88-temple Shikoku pilgrimage, Dogo Onsen, and the Naruto whirlpools. The pace is relaxed and community spirit is warm. Schools are smaller with better student-to-teacher ratios, allowing more individual attention — ideal for focused, immersive study.
shikoku.climate: The Seto Inland Sea side is warm with little rain; the Pacific side (Kochi) is warm but rainy. Four seasons: summers 28–33°C, winters 5–10°C.
shikoku.suitableFor: Students who want small-class attention, a quiet and focused environment, enjoy nature and hot springs, or are looking for the best value-for-money study experience in Japan.
shikoku.lifeAccess: Takamatsu and Matsuyama have local transport and tram lines; expressway bridges connect to Honshu. The pace of life is slow, and rents and living costs are among the lowest in Japan.

kyushu.label: Kyushu & Okinawa
kyushu.description: Kyushu comprises seven prefectures plus Okinawa. Fukuoka — the region's largest city — is a rising study-abroad hotspot with great amenities and affordable costs. Nagasaki has deep multicultural history, Kumamoto has the spectacular Aso volcano, and Okinawa is a subtropical island paradise. Warm climate, excellent food, and friendly prices combine urban convenience with a distinctly southern character.
kyushu.climate: Warm overall: Kyushu main island has four seasons (summers 30–35°C, winters 6–12°C); Okinawa is subtropical with warm weather year-round (18–30°C).
kyushu.suitableFor: Students who like warm weather, want urban convenience at affordable prices, are interested in connecting with Asia (close to Korea and Taiwan), or love food and island life.
kyushu.lifeAccess: Fukuoka has a subway and an airport minutes from the city center, with frequent flights to Taiwan. Daily amenities are solid, and rents and living costs are relatively affordable.

hero.title: Frequently Asked Questions
hero.sub: Answers to the most common questions about studying and working in Japan, so you can prepare with confidence.

aside.title: Talk to one of our consultants
aside.body: Whether it's the application process, budget planning, or Japan work visa questions — our consultants are here to help.

0.q: Can I study in Japan with no Japanese ability?
0.a:
For short-term study (visa-exempt entry), yes — you can absolutely start from scratch with just the Japanese alphabet.

However, if you plan to apply for long-term study of 6 months or more (student visa), Japan's Immigration Services Agency has tightened its requirements. The old '150-hour study certificate' is no longer accepted.

For a long-term visa, we now recommend having at least JLPT N5 (or passing the school's Japanese placement interview).

1.q: What's the difference between short-term and long-term study?
1.a: The key differences lie in duration, visa type, and core purpose. Choose based on your goals:

0.title: Short-Term Study (2 weeks – 3 months)
0.desc: Ideal for using school holidays, paid leave, or a career transition gap to improve spoken Japanese and experience daily life in Japan. No study visa required — Taiwanese passport holders can enter visa-free for up to 90 days, making this the easiest first step into life in Japan.

1.title: Long-Term Study (6 months – 2 years)
1.desc: Best for those aiming to reach fluent Japanese (JLPT N2/N1 or above), or planning to pursue higher education or a career in Japan. Requires a 'Student' residence status (student visa). Benefits include full academic and career support, plus the legal right to work part-time (up to 28 hours/week) to help cover living costs.

2.q: How do I choose the right language school?
2.a: The key is matching the school to your study purpose and personal preferences. Consider these dimensions:

0.title: Teaching Style
0.desc: Do you want practical everyday conversation, or a school focused on exam prep and university entrance (JLPT, EJU)?

1.title: City & Lifestyle
1.desc: Do you prefer the energy and resources of a major city like Tokyo or Osaka, or a smaller city with lower costs and a more relaxed pace?

2.title: Nationality Mix
2.desc: Do you want a diverse international student body, or a community with more Mandarin-speaking peers for mutual support?

3.q: How are agency fees calculated? What costs should I prepare for?
3.a: HAOGAKU's services are completely free for students — we charge zero agency fees. All tuition is paid directly to the Japanese school at their official rates, with no markups or hidden charges. The main costs you need to prepare for are:

0.title: School Fees
0.desc: Tuition, application fee, enrollment fee, and materials fee.

1.title: Living Expenses
1.desc: Accommodation, daily living costs, flights, and overseas insurance.

4.q: Is dormitory included in the tuition?
4.a:
No — accommodation is a separate cost.

Japanese schools offer a wide variety of housing options, typically ranging from ¥30,000 to ¥90,000 per month depending on the city, neighborhood, and room type (single vs. shared).

Beyond school dorms, we also have long-term partnerships with local rental networks and student apartment providers that don't require a guarantor.

Before you apply, our consultants will walk you through all accommodation options and costs based on your budget.

5.q: How long does the visa process take? What's the approval rate?
5.a:
Japan's student visa (Certificate of Eligibility, COE) review typically takes 2–3 months.

To allow plenty of time, we strongly recommend starting the application process 5–6 months before your intended enrollment date.

Japan's immigration authority applies strict standards for long-term visas. The most critical factors are the quality of your 'Study Purpose Statement' and the completeness of your financial documentation.

Students who follow our consultant's guidance step-by-step have an excellent track record of approval — there's no need to worry excessively about the rate.

6.q: What if I get sick in Japan? Is health insurance expensive?
6.a:
Students on a long-term student visa (6 months or more) are legally required to enroll in Japan's National Health Insurance (Kokumin Kenko Hoken).

Once enrolled, you typically only pay 30% of medical costs, covering standard consultations, prescriptions, and basic dental care. Premiums are calculated based on your declared income from the previous year in Japan.

Since newly arrived students have no prior-year income on record, premiums are usually heavily reduced — often as low as ¥1,000–2,000 per month.

We cover the full process for registering at your local ward office (kuyakusho) during our pre-departure orientation.

7.q: Can I work part-time while studying in Japan?
7.a:
Yes. As long as you hold a long-term student visa and obtain 'Permission to Engage in Activity Other than That Permitted' (資格外活動許可) — either at the airport on arrival or afterward at an immigration office — you can work legally. Japanese law caps student part-time work at 28 hours per week (up to 8 hours/day and 40 hours/week during school holidays).

Minimum wages vary by region. In major cities like Tokyo and Osaka, hourly rates are roughly ¥1,100–1,300; in smaller cities, around ¥950–1,050. Part-time work not only helps with daily expenses — it's one of the best ways to build spoken Japanese and integrate into Japanese society.

8.q: Can I stay in Japan to work after graduating from a language school?
8.a: Yes — but successfully obtaining a Japanese work visa depends primarily on your educational background and Japanese ability:

0.title: Educational Background
0.desc: You must hold a Taiwanese college diploma (associate degree, bachelor's, or above), or have completed a Japanese vocational school program or higher.

1.title: Japanese Language Requirement
1.desc: Under Japan's latest immigration guidelines, if your target role involves communication-based duties (e.g. sales, translation, business services, hospitality management) and the employer is a small-to-medium Japanese company, JLPT N2 (CEFR B2) or above will be mandatory when applying for a work visa.

hero.title: Take Your First Step in 2 Weeks to 3 Months

whatIs.title: What Is Short-Term Study?
whatIs.body:
Short-term study means staying in Japan for 2 weeks to 3 months, with a focus on language learning and authentic local life experience.

The biggest advantage? No long-term student visa required. Students simply enter on a tourist visa-exempt basis (up to 90 days with a Taiwanese passport).

Whether you want to ease into life in Japan before committing to a longer program, or make the most of a short break, this is the most flexible and stress-free way to start your Japan journey.

0.title: Working Professionals Recharging
0.desc: Use paid leave or a career transition break to push through plateaus in spoken Japanese and listening in a full-immersion environment.

1.title: Students Making the Most of Holidays
1.desc: Step beyond the textbook during summer or winter break for a deep, hands-on experience of everyday life in Japan.

2.title: Planners Considering Japan Long-Term
2.desc: Experience Japan in person before committing to a long-term visa application — and confirm whether the lifestyle suits you.

3.title: Japan Enthusiasts Who Want More Than Tourism
3.desc: Not just sightseeing. Live like a local and explore Japanese culture through daily life.

features.title: Program Features
features.body:
Short-term courses focus on intensive, practical Japanese. Classes typically run 3–4 hours per day in small groups of just 4–10 students, giving you maximum progress in speaking and listening within a full-immersion environment.

Beyond classroom training, schools regularly organize cultural experiences like tea ceremony, kimono wearing, and field trips. You'll also connect with international students from around the world — learning that goes well beyond textbooks, helping you naturally blend into Japanese daily life and build a global perspective.

cost.title: Cost & Duration Reference
cost.body: Short-term programs are highly flexible — choose anywhere from 2 to 12 weeks:

2.title: Estimated Total
2.desc: Including flights and basic living costs, total budget is roughly NT$35,000–280,000 (varies by duration, city, and personal spending habits).

reminder.title: Helpful Reminder
reminder.body: Short-term language school programs in Japan typically open enrollment each quarter (January, April, July, and October). Spots and dormitory places are limited — we recommend contacting our consultants at least 3 months before your intended departure to secure the best schedule for you.

whatIs.title: What Is Long-Term Study?
whatIs.body:
Long-term study means enrolling in a Japanese language school for 6 months to 2 years while applying for a 'Student' residence status (student visa). Compared to short-term programs, this gives you the time to bring your Japanese to genuine fluency and build real local connections.

Better yet, you can legally work part-time (up to 28 hours per week) — earning money to help cover living costs while gaining first-hand experience of Japanese work culture.

0.title: Serious Japanese Learners with Clear Goals
0.desc: For those committed to reaching genuine fluency — N2 or N1 level — through total immersion in a full Japanese-language environment.

1.title: Future Japan-Based Professionals
1.desc: Planning to work or change careers in Japan and looking to build solid business communication skills and adapt to Japanese workplace culture first.

2.title: Applicants Preparing for Higher Education
2.desc: Aiming for a Japanese university, graduate school, or vocational school and needing a dedicated transition period for exam prep and academic support.

3.title: Japan Enthusiasts Seeking Deep Immersion
3.desc: Ready to take a meaningful gap year — spending 1 to 2 years living fully in Japan to explore what comes next in life.

features.title: Program Features
features.body:
Long-term programs center on comprehensive academic and practical Japanese, using a structured progression from foundational to advanced levels. Students build intuitive listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills in a total-immersion environment.

At the intermediate and advanced stages, courses integrate targeted JLPT exam preparation, business Japanese, and academic writing — tailored to each student's career goals.

Schools also offer dedicated one-on-one support for university applications and job hunting, covering everything from school applications and resume editing to mock interviews. Regular cultural events and international exchange activities help students integrate deeply into Japanese society and build lasting networks.

process.title: Application Timeline
process.body: To secure your visa and enroll on schedule, the long-term study application process typically requires starting 4–6 months in advance:

0.title: 4–6 Months Before Enrollment
0.desc: Assess your goals, confirm your intake term, and select your ideal school.

1.title: 3–4 Months Before Enrollment
1.desc: Prepare complete written application documents and submit them to the school for review.

2.title: 1–2 Months Before Enrollment
2.desc: The school submits the application to Japan's Immigration Services Agency on your behalf to obtain the Certificate of Eligibility (COE).

3.title: 1 Month Before Departure
3.desc: Bring your original COE, passport, and ID to the Japan-Taiwan Exchange Association to apply for your study visa — typically processed within 2–5 business days. Once your visa is issued and accommodation and flights are arranged, you're ready to go.

cost.title: Cost Reference
cost.body: Long-term programs typically run from 6 months to 2 years. Choose the length that fits your goals:

2.title: Estimated Total
2.desc: Including flights and basic living costs, a full year's budget is roughly NT$350,000–600,000 (varies by city, accommodation type, and personal spending habits).

documents.title: Required Documents
documents.body: A complete set of written materials is required for a long-term study application. All documents must be current and accurate:

0.title: Personal Documents
0.desc: Passport copy, compliant personal photo, application form, and a detailed study purpose statement.

1.title: Academic Records
1.desc: Original graduation certificate and official transcripts from your highest level of completed education.

2.title: Financial Proof
2.desc: Bank statements showing a balance of at least NT$800,000–1,000,000, plus the financial sponsor's employment certificate and annual income documentation (e.g. tax withholding certificate).

howWeHelp.title: How HAOGAKU Supports You
howWeHelp.body:
Long-term language school programs in Japan primarily open each spring (April) and autumn (October), with some schools also accepting intake in January and July.

Since long-term study requires applying for residence status with the Japanese government, the process involves considerable paperwork — and school spots and dormitories fill up quickly. We recommend reaching out to our consultants 4–6 months before your intended departure so we can map out the smoothest visa and enrollment timeline for you.

hero.title: Earn a Degree in Japan — Build the Foundation for Your Future Career
hero.sub: From language school to vocational school or university — HAOGAKU plans every step with you.

whatIs.title: What Is Higher Education Abroad?
whatIs.body: Higher education abroad means, after completing foundational Japanese language study, going on to enroll in a Japanese vocational school, university, or graduate school to earn an official academic degree or professional diploma — typically a 2 to 4-year commitment. Unlike a language school, this path lets students specialize deeply in a specific field (such as anime, design, business, or engineering) and earn an internationally recognized qualification. Graduates not only possess strong professional skills and Japanese fluency, but also significantly improve their competitiveness in the Japanese job market — with a clear pathway to convert a student visa into a 'Technology / Humanities / International Services' work visa and launch a career in Japan.

0.title: Hands-On Learners Pursuing a Specialty
0.desc: Planning to enroll in a vocational school to build practical skills in anime, design, pharmaceuticals, IT, or beauty — laying a solid foundation for the next step in your career.

1.title: Students Dreaming of a Japanese University
1.desc: Looking to enter Japan's higher education system, experience full campus life, and earn a bachelor's degree with international recognition.

2.title: Researchers Pursuing Advanced Study
2.desc: Targeting a Japanese graduate school to conduct in-depth research in a specific academic field and pursue a master's or doctoral degree.

3.title: Planners with an Eye on the Japanese Job Market
3.desc: Aiming to work directly in a Japanese company after graduation, leveraging a local Japanese qualification and the school's industry connections to land a job.

features.title: Program Features
features.body: Japan's higher education institutions are renowned for rigorous academic training and close industry collaboration. Vocational schools emphasize 'job-ready' skills, with hands-on instruction from frontline industry professionals and robust internship opportunities. Universities and graduate schools provide comprehensive research resources and academic environments that cultivate critical thinking and problem-solving at the highest level. During the application preparation phase, beyond achieving JLPT N2 or N1 proficiency, the focus shifts to intensive preparation for the Examination for Japanese University Admission for International Students (EJU), school-specific entrance exams (written tests and essays), and professor interviews. Through systematic application planning and expert guidance, students gain a precise understanding of each school's admissions criteria, sharpen their academic writing and logical reasoning, and maximize their chances of gaining entry to their target institution.

process.title: Application Timeline
process.body: To successfully gain admission to your target school, preparation for higher education typically needs to begin 8–12 months in advance:

0.title: Summer–Autumn of the Year Before Enrollment (usually April)
0.desc: Students must first achieve qualifying EJU or JLPT scores, then submit written application materials — including the admission application and research student form — during the autumn–winter period (4–6 months before enrollment).

1.title: After Passing Document Review and Entrance Exams
1.desc: The school sends an acceptance letter 2–3 months before enrollment. After confirming enrollment and paying fees, students already in Japan apply to change their residence status; students applying directly from Taiwan follow the standard COE process to obtain a student visa.

2.title: Approximately 3 Months Before the April Start Date
2.desc: Arrange accommodation and flights — then head to Japan for the April enrollment.

cost.title: Cost Reference
cost.body: Higher education programs typically run 2–4 years (vocational schools and graduate schools around 2 years; universities around 4 years). Budget estimates vary based on the type of institution:

0.title: Tuition & Fees
0.desc: National and public universities: approximately ¥500,000–800,000/year. Private universities or vocational schools: approximately ¥900,000–1,500,000/year (roughly NT$180,000–300,000; science and medical-related programs are typically higher).

2.title: Estimated Total
2.desc: Including flights and basic living costs, an annual budget of roughly NT$500,000–850,000 (varies by institution type, city, and personal spending habits).

documents.title: Required Documents
documents.body: Japanese higher education institutions require a rigorous and complete set of written materials. For basic personal documents, students need a passport copy, compliant personal photo, application form, and a detailed statement of purpose. For academic and language credentials, original graduation certificates and transcripts from the highest level of completed education are required, along with recent language proficiency proof (JLPT certificate, EJU score report; some universities also require TOEFL or TOEIC scores). Graduate school applicants must additionally prepare a 'Research Proposal' and a letter of recommendation from a supervising professor; applicants to art or design vocational schools typically need to submit a portfolio. Financial proof (bank statements and the financial sponsor's employment certificate) is also a key document for both visa and admission review.

reminder.title: Helpful Reminder
reminder.body: The vast majority of Japanese universities and vocational schools begin in spring (April), and each school's application window is short and strictly enforced — typically falling in the autumn to winter of the year before enrollment. Since the process involves complex exam registration, research proposal writing, and school outreach, we recommend students contact our consultants 8–12 months before their intended enrollment, and confirm their target programs and eligibility requirements as early as possible, so we can build a solid, customized application strategy and timeline.

cooperation.title: Cooperation Model & Role Definition
cooperation.desc: Clarifies our role in cross-border workforce collaboration and how we work with licensed Japanese employment agencies.
cooperation.category: For Japanese employment agencies and human resource partners
cooperation.alt: Japan recruitment agency cooperation overseas workforce matching
cooperation.q1: What role do you play in the overall process?
cooperation.a1: We act as a matching and coordination partner, connecting Southeast Asian sending organizations, Taiwan-based human resources, and licensed Japanese employment agencies. Our role focuses on early-stage candidate information整理, condition alignment, and partner matching. We do not conduct employment placement or statutory procedures in Japan.
cooperation.q2: Do you replace the role of Japanese employment agencies?
cooperation.a2: No. We do not conduct employment placement activities in Japan. All formal job placement, employment contracts, and residence status procedures are handled exclusively by licensed Japanese employment agencies.
cooperation.q3: What types of partners are suitable for cooperation?
cooperation.a3: Our services are suitable for Japanese employment agencies that already handle or plan to handle overseas workforce cases, as well as partners seeking to expand their options for Southeast Asian or Taiwanese talent.
cooperation.q4: Can cooperation start with a single case?
cooperation.a4: Yes. Most collaborations begin with a single case or a backup staffing need. No exclusive or long-term commitment is required.
cooperation.q5: Is it necessary to sign a long-term or exclusive agreement?
cooperation.a5: No. Cooperation is conducted on a case-by-case basis to maintain flexibility and avoid interference with existing partnerships.
cooperation.q6: Is cooperation still possible if we already work with a fixed Southeast Asian sending organization?
cooperation.a6: Yes. We often act as a secondary or backup option, supporting cases that existing sending organizations may find difficult to handle or are temporarily unable to supply.
cooperation.q7: Do you directly contact Japanese corporate clients?
cooperation.a7: This depends on the cooperation model. When cases are led by a Japanese employment agency, we participate as a backend support and coordination partner without affecting existing client relationships.
cooperation.q8: Who communicates with which parties during cooperation?
cooperation.a8: We primarily coordinate with Southeast Asian sending organizations and Taiwan-side partners. Communication with Japanese companies and formal placement processes remains led by the Japanese employment agency.
cooperation.q9: Can we exchange information first before deciding on cooperation?
cooperation.a9: Yes. We encourage initial information exchange regarding cases or candidate conditions before determining further cooperation.

resources.title: Talent Sources & Matching Scope
resources.desc: Introduces available talent sources and suitable case types for cooperation.
resources.category: For partners interested in talent sourcing flexibility
resources.alt: Southeast Asia talent Taiwan talent overseas workforce sources
resources.q1: What talent sources can you provide?
resources.a1: Our primary sources are Southeast Asian talents (such as Vietnam and Indonesia). Depending on case requirements, we can also provide Taiwanese talent as a supplementary option.
resources.q2: Are there additional introduction fees for Southeast Asian talent?
resources.a2: The Southeast Asian sending organizations we cooperate with are long-term partners of Taiwanese enterprises. Therefore, no additional introduction fees are charged to the Japanese side.
resources.q3: Are you limited to specific industries or job categories?
resources.a3: No. However, suitability for overseas talent is evaluated during the early-stage assessment based on actual job content, working conditions, and management structure.
resources.q4: Can you act as a secondary or backup talent source?
resources.a4: Yes. We frequently serve as a backup option alongside existing sending organizations, particularly for cases with special conditions or higher risk.
resources.q5: Is it possible to compare multiple nationalities or sources simultaneously?
resources.a5: Yes. We can provide recommendations across multiple talent sources based on case conditions to support comparison and decision-making.
resources.q6: Can you support situations where talent supply is unstable?
resources.a6: One of our roles is to fill supply gaps by offering alternative options when existing channels cannot provide candidates in time.
resources.q7: Do you help evaluate whether a position is suitable for overseas talent?
resources.a7: Yes. Before entering the formal placement process, we can conduct an early-stage feasibility assessment of the position.
resources.q8: Do you handle short-term or part-time-only cases?
resources.a8: Our focus is on full-time positions eligible for lawful residence status. We do not handle cases limited to part-time work or short-term internships.

scope.title: Scope of Responsibility & Post-Placement Support
scope.desc: Clarifies service boundaries and available support after placement.
scope.category: For partners focused on risk management and clear role allocation
scope.alt: Overseas workforce post-placement support cooperation scope
scope.q1: Do you assist with post-placement issues?
scope.a1: If communication or adaptation issues arise after placement, we can coordinate with sending organizations and relevant parties to provide informational support and adjustment assistance. However, we do not assume statutory management responsibilities in Japan.
scope.q2: Do you handle labor management or labor disputes?
scope.a2: No. Labor management and legal responsibilities are handled in accordance with Japanese law by the employer and licensed employment agency.
scope.q3: Do you handle visa or residence status applications?
scope.a3: No. Visa and residence status applications are handled by licensed Japanese employment agencies or certified administrative scriveners.
scope.q4: How are issues handled during cooperation?
scope.a4: Our role is to facilitate communication and coordination, ensure transparency of information, and support partners in quickly clarifying situations so that each party can respond in compliance with applicable regulations.
scope.q5: Do you provide regular follow-ups or feedback mechanisms?
scope.a5: Periodic information feedback can be arranged based on case requirements to help track talent adaptation.
scope.q6: If a worker leaves early, are you responsible for replacement?
scope.a6: Replacement arrangements depend on the contract between the Japanese employment agency and the employer. We can assist with subsequent communication and matching support.
scope.q7: Do you provide any employment outcome guarantees?
scope.a7: No. We do not provide employment outcome guarantees. Our responsibility is limited to matching and coordination support.
scope.q8: Can you help establish long-term cooperation processes?
scope.a8: Yes. Based on cooperation experience, we can assist in organizing repeatable workflows and communication frameworks.

stortText: “Formosa” is more than just a place name — it's where we began. As a Taiwan-based recruitment agency, FORMA is dedicated to bridging cultural and geographic boundaries by connecting talents from Taiwan and Asia with Japanese companies seeking global growth. We specialize in study-abroad support, language school placement, and manpower services in Japan, offering comprehensive solutions from school applications and pre-departure guidance to local support and Specified Skilled Worker job matching. At FORMA, we believe that every step across borders opens the door to new possibilities.
